## Identifying the features (Y components)

The Y versions don't map directly to bit positions, so I matched each one to the data:

- **Y1 = bit 3:** in X6-Y1-Z1 and X6-Y1-Z4, the button depends only on whether the two bit-3 values are the same or differ.
- **Y2 = bit 1:** in X6-Y2-Z1, the button depends only on whether the two bit-1 values are the same or differ.
- **Y3 = bit 2:** in X3-Y3-Z1, button 3 appears exactly when both bit-2s are 1. In X2-Y3-Z3, button 0 appears exactly when neither bit-2 is 1.
- **Y4 = bit 4:** in X3-Y4-Z2, button 3 appears exactly when both bit-4s are 1.

## Rules and button mappings (X and Z)

What the data pins down:

- Under Z1, bits that differ give 3 and bits that are the same give 0.
- Under Z1, both bits being 1 gives 3 and anything else gives 0.
- Under Z3, at least one bit being 1 gives 1 and neither gives 0.

Two assignments fit all six known tasks:

- **A:** Z1 gives 3 when true and 0 when false. X3 = "both are 1", X6 = "exactly one is 1".
- **B:** Z1 gives 0 when true and 3 when false. X3 = "not both are 1", X6 = "both are the same".

Independently, X2 is either "at least one is 1" (Z3 gives 1 when true) or "neither is 1" (Z3 gives 0 when true).

## The new task, X2-Y4-Z1

This looks at bit 4 in both stimuli. Combining the options gives only two possible answer sets:

| Assignment | At least one bit 4 is 1 | Neither bit 4 is 1 |
|---|---|---|
| A + "at least one" | 3 | 0 |
| B + "neither" | 3 | 0 |
| A + "neither" | 0 | 3 |
| B + "at least one" | 0 | 3 |

I looked for a cross-component pattern, such as "true always maps to the higher button," but none holds in every case. I prefer assignment A with X2 = "at least one is 1", because those are the most natural readings: X3 = "both", X2 = "at least one", and Z1 giving 3 when true. That gives:

**At least one bit 4 is 1 → button 3; otherwise → button 0.**

| # | Input | Bit 4 values | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0010 0000 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1010 1110 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 0101 0010 | 1, 0 | 3 |
| 4 | 1010 0100 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 0000 0110 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 6 | 0100 0111 | 0, 1 | 3 |
| 7 | 0011 1010 | 1, 0 | 3 |
| 8 | 0101 0001 | 1, 1 | 3 |
| 9 | 1110 1111 | 0, 1 | 3 |
| 10 | 0100 1000 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 11 | 0100 0010 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 12 | 0001 0101 | 1, 1 | 3 |
| 13 | 1110 0100 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| 14 | 0001 1101 | 1, 1 | 3 |
| 15 | 1101 1100 | 1, 0 | 3 |
| 16 | 0010 0011 | 0, 1 | 3 |

The examples don't decide between this answer set and its exact opposite (0 and 3 swapped everywhere), so the answers are not uniquely determined.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
